records.source: Διώκετε τὴν ἀγάπην, ζηλοῦτε δὲ τὰ πνευματικά, μᾶλλον δὲ ἵνα προφητεύητε.
records.gloss: Pursue the love, be zealous but [for] the spiritual [things], rather but that you may prophesy.
pieces: Strive for love, and set your hearts on spiritual gifts, most of all on prophesying.

L.1: Pursue love, and be zealous for the spiritual [gifts], but especially that you may prophesy.

R.1: Above everything else, work hard at loving others. And try hard to receive the gifts that the Spirit gives, most of all the gift of prophecy, speaking messages from God.

decisions.choice: pursue love: make love the goal, and go after it with effort
decisions.reason: Διώκετε is the verb for running after something, pursuing it (Romans 14:19; Philippians 3:12, 14). It joins chapter 13 to chapter 14: love is the aim, and the gifts are to be sought within it.

decisions.choice: the spiritual things: the gifts the Spirit gives
decisions.reason: τὰ πνευματικά is the neuter plural of the adjective used in 12:1. Here it is what the Corinthians are to be zealous for, as the greater gifts are in 12:31, so the gifts are meant.

decisions.choice: especially that you may prophesy: of all the gifts, prophecy is the one to seek most
alternatives: instead of seeking the gifts, seek to prophesy
decisions.reason: μᾶλλον δὲ marks what is preferred. Paul is not setting prophecy against the other gifts, which he has just told them to seek, but ranking it first; verses 2-5 give the reason.

decisions.choice: be zealous for: seek eagerly, set one's heart on
decisions.reason: As in 12:31, where the same verb ζηλοῦτε is used for the greater gifts; it returns in 14:39. It is a good eagerness here, not rivalry.

decisions.choice: set your hearts on (B); try hard to receive (R)
decisions.reason: The same words as in 12:31 and 14:39, so that readers can see Paul take up the command again.

decisions.choice: the spiritual [gifts] (L); spiritual gifts (B); the gifts that the Spirit gives (R)
decisions.reason: As in 12:1, the levels supply 'gifts' (m2).

decisions.choice: speaking messages from God
decisions.reason: Readable explains what prophecy is, as at 11:4, since many readers think only of predicting the future.

records.heading: Prophecy builds up the church

records.source: ὁ γὰρ λαλῶν γλώσσῃ οὐκ ἀνθρώποις λαλεῖ ἀλλὰ θεῷ, οὐδεὶς γὰρ ἀκούει, πνεύματι δὲ λαλεῖ μυστήρια·
records.gloss: The [one] for speaking in a tongue not to people speaks but to God; no one for hears, in spirit but he speaks mysteries;
pieces: Someone who speaks in a tongue is speaking not to people but to God. No one understands what is said; in the Spirit, the speaker is uttering mysteries.

L.2: For the one speaking in a tongue speaks not to people but to God, for no one understands; but in [the] Spirit [the speaker] utters mysteries.

R.2: When people speak in tongues, they are not speaking to other people. They are speaking to God. No one else can understand them. The Spirit is helping them speak, but what they say is a mystery to everyone else.

decisions.choice: speaks to God: a tongue is addressed to God, in prayer or praise
alternatives: a tongue is a message from God to people
decisions.reason: Verses 14-17 speak of praying, singing and giving thanks in a tongue: the speech goes up to God. That is why it does not build up others unless it is interpreted (verse 5).

decisions.choice: hears: understands
decisions.reason: Those present hear the sound; ἀκούει means that no one grasps what is said, as the same verb is used in the Greek Old Testament of Genesis 11:7, where the builders of Babel can no longer understand one another's speech.

decisions.choice: in the Spirit: the Holy Spirit gives the speech
alternatives: in his spirit: with the speaker's own spirit rather than the mind (verse 14)
decisions.reason: πνεύματι has neither an article nor 'my', so it could mean either. The Spirit is the one who gives tongues (12:10-11), which favors the Holy Spirit. Verse 14 ('my spirit prays') speaks of the speaker's own spirit, which favors the other reading. The two are close: in a tongue the speaker's spirit is moved by God's Spirit.

decisions.choice: mysteries: things hidden from the hearers, because no one understands them
alternatives: God's plan, once hidden and now made known, as in 2:7 and 15:51
decisions.reason: Elsewhere in Paul μυστήρια usually names God's purpose now revealed. Here the point is that the words stay hidden from those who hear them.

decisions.choice: mysteries (L, B); a mystery to everyone else (R)
decisions.reason: The key term 'mystery' is kept at every level, with its sense here given in m4. Readable says to whom it is a mystery.

decisions.choice: in [the] Spirit [the speaker] utters
decisions.reason: Literal supplies the article and a subject, which the Greek verb leaves unexpressed.

decisions.choice: The Spirit is helping them speak
decisions.reason: Readable says what 'in the Spirit' means, following m3. Since m3 is uncertain, this is marked for reviewers.

records.source: ὁ δὲ προφητεύων ἀνθρώποις λαλεῖ οἰκοδομὴν καὶ παράκλησιν καὶ παραμυθίαν.
records.gloss: The [one] but prophesying to people speaks building up and encouragement and comfort.
pieces: But someone who prophesies speaks to people, and the words build them up, encourage them and comfort them.

L.3: But the one prophesying speaks to people [for] building up and encouragement and comfort.

R.3: But people who prophesy speak to others. What they say helps others grow stronger, gives them courage, and comforts them.

decisions.choice: building up: making the church grow strong, like a building rising on its foundation
decisions.reason: οἰκοδομὴν is the act of building. Paul pictures the church as God's building (3:9-10) and speaks of love building up (8:1; 10:23). The word runs through this chapter (verses 3-5, 12, 17, 26) as the test of every gift.

decisions.choice: encouragement and comfort: urging on, and consoling those who are downcast
decisions.reason: παράκλησιν can mean comfort, appeal or encouragement, and it is the word for comfort in 2 Corinthians 1:3-7. Here it stands beside παραμυθίαν, consolation for those who grieve or lose heart (as in Philippians 2:1), so it has its other sense, encouragement.

decisions.choice: to people: unlike a tongue, prophecy is understood by those who hear it
decisions.reason: The contrast with verse 2 is exact: the one speaks to God, the other to people.

decisions.choice: building up (L); build them up (B); helps others grow stronger (R)
decisions.reason: 'Build up' keeps Paul's picture of a building, as in 8:1, 10:23 and 2 Corinthians 10:8; 'edification' is now church language. Readable says 'grow stronger' throughout the chapter, as 8:1 says 'makes others strong'.

decisions.choice: [for] building up
decisions.reason: The Greek makes the three nouns the object of 'speaks'; Literal supplies 'for' to show that they name what the speech does.

records.source: ὁ λαλῶν γλώσσῃ ἑαυτὸν οἰκοδομεῖ· ὁ δὲ προφητεύων ἐκκλησίαν οἰκοδομεῖ.
records.gloss: The [one] speaking in a tongue himself builds up; the [one] but prophesying [the] church builds up.
pieces: Those who speak in a tongue build up themselves, but those who prophesy build up the church.

L.4: The one speaking in a tongue builds up {{gender:themselves|himself}}, but the one prophesying builds up [the] church.

R.4: People who speak in tongues help only themselves grow stronger. But people who prophesy help the whole church grow stronger.

decisions.choice: builds up himself: a real benefit, but for the speaker alone
alternatives: a rebuke of a self-centered use of the gift
decisions.reason: Paul does not say that being built up oneself is wrong: he goes on to wish that all spoke in tongues (verse 5) and thanks God for his own gift (verse 18). But the gifts are given for the good of all (12:7), so in the gathering a gift that helps only its user is the lesser.

decisions.choice: church: the believers as they gather together
decisions.reason: ἐκκλησίαν has no article: the assembly of believers when they meet. Throughout the chapter Paul has the gathering in view (verses 19, 23, 28).

decisions.choice: Those who speak ... those who prophesy (B); People who ... (R)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable use plurals, since men and women alike are meant; Literal keeps the singular with the gender setting.

decisions.choice: only themselves; the whole church
decisions.reason: Readable brings out the contrast between one person and everyone (m1).

records.source: θέλω δὲ πάντας ὑμᾶς λαλεῖν γλώσσαις, μᾶλλον δὲ ἵνα προφητεύητε· μείζων δὲ ὁ προφητεύων ἢ ὁ λαλῶν γλώσσαις, ἐκτὸς εἰ μὴ διερμηνεύῃ, ἵνα ἡ ἐκκλησία οἰκοδομὴν λάβῃ.
records.gloss: I want now all you to speak in tongues, rather but that you may prophesy; greater and the [one] prophesying than the [one] speaking in tongues, except if not he interprets, so that the church building up may receive.
pieces: I would be glad for all of you to speak in tongues, but gladder still for you to prophesy. Those who prophesy are greater than those who speak in tongues, unless they also interpret, so that the church receives something that builds it up.

L.5: Now I want all of you to speak in tongues, but rather that you may prophesy; and the one prophesying [is] greater than the one speaking in tongues, unless [the speaker] interprets, so that the church may receive building up.

R.5: I would like every one of you to speak in tongues, but I would much rather have you prophesy. Prophesying is more important than speaking in tongues, unless the speakers also interpret what they say. Then the whole church can grow stronger.

decisions.choice: I want all of you to speak in tongues: a real wish, though prophecy is the greater one
alternatives: a concession: 'I grant that you may all speak in tongues'
decisions.reason: Paul values the gift (verses 18, 39) and does not forbid it. But μᾶλλον δὲ ('but rather') sets the greater wish beside the lesser one, as in verse 1. The wish recalls Moses' wish that all God's people were prophets (Numbers 11:29).

decisions.choice: greater: of more use to the church
decisions.reason: The last clause gives the measure: the church is built up. μείζων takes up 'the greater gifts' of 12:31.

decisions.choice: unless he interprets: the one who spoke in the tongue also interprets it
decisions.reason: διερμηνεύῃ has no stated subject. The nearest person is the one speaking in tongues, and verse 13 tells such a person to pray to interpret; verse 27 allows another to do it. Either way the condition is that the tongue is understood.

decisions.choice: I would be glad ... but gladder still
decisions.reason: Balanced shows the two wishes as lesser and greater (m1).

decisions.choice: [the speaker] (L); the speakers also interpret what they say (R)
decisions.reason: Literal and Readable name the subject chosen in m3; Balanced says 'they also interpret'.

records.source: Νῦν δέ, ἀδελφοί, ἐὰν ἔλθω πρὸς ὑμᾶς γλώσσαις λαλῶν, τί ὑμᾶς ὠφελήσω, ἐὰν μὴ ὑμῖν λαλήσω ἢ ἐν ἀποκαλύψει ἢ ἐν γνώσει ἢ ἐν προφητείᾳ ἢ ἐν διδαχῇ;
records.gloss: Now but, brothers, if I come to you in tongues speaking, what you will I benefit, if not to you I speak either in revelation or in knowledge or in prophecy or in teaching?
pieces: So then, {{gender:brothers and sisters|brothers}}, suppose I come to you speaking in tongues. What use will I be to you, unless what I say to you brings a revelation, or knowledge, or prophecy, or teaching?

L.6: But now, {{gender:brothers and sisters|brothers}}, if I come to you speaking in tongues, what will I profit you, unless I speak to you either in revelation or in knowledge or in prophecy or in teaching?

R.6: {{gender:Brothers and sisters|Brothers}}, suppose I came to visit you and spoke only in tongues. That would not help you at all. To help you, I would need to bring you a revelation from God, or knowledge, or prophecy, or teaching.

decisions.choice: but now: as things are, to come to the point
decisions.reason: Νῦν here draws a conclusion, as in 12:18 and 12:20; it is not about time. Paul now applies verses 1-5 to himself.

decisions.choice: if I come: an example Paul imagines, not a planned visit
decisions.reason: Paul makes himself the test case: even an apostle speaking in tongues would do the church no good.

decisions.choice: revelation, knowledge, prophecy, teaching: kinds of speech the church can understand
alternatives: two pairs: revelation given through prophecy, and knowledge given through teaching
decisions.reason: Paul names four kinds of understandable speech. Some take them as two pairs, an inner gift and the speech that brings it out, but the Greek simply lists them with 'or'. Revelation and teaching come back in the list of verse 26; knowledge and prophecy are gifts named in 12:8-10.

decisions.choice: That would not help you at all.
decisions.reason: Readable gives the answer the question expects.

decisions.choice: a revelation from God
decisions.reason: Readable says who gives the revelation.

records.source: ὅμως τὰ ἄψυχα φωνὴν διδόντα, εἴτε αὐλὸς εἴτε κιθάρα, ἐὰν διαστολὴν τοῖς φθόγγοις μὴ δῷ, πῶς γνωσθήσεται τὸ αὐλούμενον ἢ τὸ κιθαριζόμενον;
records.gloss: Likewise the lifeless [things] a sound giving, whether flute or harp, if a distinction to the notes not they give, how will be known the being piped or the being harped?
pieces: Think of instruments, lifeless as they are, that give out a sound, like the flute or the harp. If their notes are not distinct, how can anyone tell what is being played on the flute or the harp?

L.7: Likewise lifeless [things] that give a sound, whether flute or harp: if they do not give a distinction in the notes, how will what is piped or what is harped be known?

R.7: Musical instruments like the flute and the harp are not alive, but they make sounds. If each note does not sound clear and different, no one can tell what tune is being played.

decisions.choice: likewise: in the same way, introducing a comparison
decisions.reason: ὅμως usually means 'nevertheless', but here, as in Galatians 3:15, it introduces a comparison, and some read it with a different accent as 'likewise'. Either way the instruments illustrate the point.

decisions.choice: flute and harp: a wind instrument and a stringed instrument of the Greek world
decisions.reason: The αὐλὸς was a reed pipe, often played in pairs, heard at feasts, weddings, funerals and in the worship of the gods. The κιθάρα was a lyre with a wooden sound box, plucked with the fingers or a pick. Paul names the most common instruments.

decisions.choice: a distinction in the notes: notes that differ from one another, so that a tune can be heard
decisions.reason: διαστολὴν is a difference or separation; φθόγγοις are musical sounds. A tune is heard only when the notes are distinct.

decisions.choice: flute, harp
decisions.reason: 'Flute' and 'harp' are the nearest instruments familiar to modern readers; m2 describes the actual instruments.

decisions.choice: no one can tell what tune is being played
decisions.reason: Readable gives the answer to the question.

records.source: καὶ γὰρ ἐὰν ἄδηλον φωνὴν σάλπιγξ δῷ, τίς παρασκευάσεται εἰς πόλεμον;
records.gloss: Also for if an unclear sound a trumpet gives, who will prepare himself for battle?
pieces: And if a trumpet sounds a signal no one can make out, who will prepare to fight?

L.8: For indeed, if a trumpet gives an unclear sound, who will prepare for battle?

R.8: In an army, a trumpet tells the soldiers to get ready for battle. But if the trumpet does not play a clear call, no one will know it is time to get ready.

decisions.choice: trumpet: an instrument used to give signals in war
decisions.reason: Armies were called to arms and given orders by trumpet calls (Numbers 10:9; Jeremiah 4:19). A call no one can recognize leaves the soldiers unprepared.

decisions.choice: who will prepare?: no one will
decisions.reason: The question expects the answer 'no one'.

decisions.choice: In an army, a trumpet tells the soldiers to get ready for battle.
decisions.reason: Readable explains what a trumpet call was for (m1) and gives the answer to the question (m2).

records.source: οὕτως καὶ ὑμεῖς διὰ τῆς γλώσσης ἐὰν μὴ εὔσημον λόγον δῶτε, πῶς γνωσθήσεται τὸ λαλούμενον;
records.gloss: So also you through the tongue if not a clear word you give, how will be known the being spoken?
pieces: So with you: if your tongue does not produce speech that makes sense, how will what you say be understood?

L.9: So also you: unless you give a clear word through the tongue, how will what is spoken be known?

R.9: It is like that for you too. When you speak, others need words they can understand. Otherwise they cannot tell what you mean.

decisions.choice: through the tongue: with the tongue as the organ of speech
decisions.reason: τῆς γλώσσης has the article, and 'through the tongue' fits the tongue in the mouth, as the instruments of verses 7-8 make sound. Paul may be playing on the word, which also names the gift; the point is the same either way: speech must be understood.

decisions.choice: clear: easily recognized, with a plain meaning
decisions.reason: εὔσημον means well marked, distinct, the opposite of the trumpet's unclear sound in verse 8.

decisions.choice: Otherwise they cannot tell what you mean.
alternatives: how will what is spoken be known?
decisions.reason: Readable turns the question into statements.

records.source: ἔσεσθε γὰρ εἰς ἀέρα λαλοῦντες.
records.gloss: You will be for into air speaking.
pieces: You will be speaking to empty air.

L.9: For you will be speaking into [the] air.

R.9: Your words will be wasted, like talking to the wind.

decisions.choice: speaking into the air: talking to no purpose
decisions.reason: Like 'beating the air' (9:26), the phrase describes effort that reaches no one.

decisions.choice: like talking to the wind
decisions.reason: Readable uses a familiar picture for words that reach no one.

records.source: τοσαῦτα εἰ τύχοι γένη φωνῶν εἰσιν ἐν κόσμῳ, καὶ οὐδὲν ἄφωνον·
records.gloss: So many, if it may happen, kinds of sounds there are in [the] world, and nothing [is] without sound;
pieces: Who knows how many languages there are in the world? And not one of them is without meaning.

L.10: There are, it may be, so many kinds of languages in [the] world, and none [is] without meaning;

R.10: There are many, many languages in the world, and every one of them means something to the people who speak it.

decisions.choice: it may be: perhaps, who knows how many
decisions.reason: εἰ τύχοι is an idiom for 'perhaps' or 'as it happens'; here it stresses that the number is great and not known.

decisions.choice: sounds: languages, human speech
decisions.reason: φωνῶν is the word used for the sound of the instruments in verses 7-8. Here the kinds of 'sound' in the world are languages, as verse 11 shows.

decisions.choice: without meaning: a play on words, literally 'soundless'
decisions.reason: ἄφωνον is formed from the same word with a negative. Here it means without meaning: every language communicates to those who know it.

decisions.choice: world: the inhabited world, humankind with its many peoples
decisions.reason: κόσμῳ here is the world of people and their languages, not the created universe or the world opposed to God.

decisions.choice: languages
decisions.reason: Every level says 'languages', since that is the sense here (m2); the gloss keeps 'sounds'.

records.source: ἐὰν οὖν μὴ εἰδῶ τὴν δύναμιν τῆς φωνῆς, ἔσομαι τῷ λαλοῦντι βάρβαρος καὶ ὁ λαλῶν ἐν ἐμοὶ βάρβαρος.
records.gloss: If therefore not I know the power of the sound, I will be to the [one] speaking a foreigner and the [one] speaking in me a foreigner.
pieces: If I do not understand the language someone speaks, we will be foreigners to each other: I to the speaker, and the speaker to me.

L.11: So if I do not know the force of the language, I will be a foreigner to the one speaking, and the one speaking [will be] a foreigner to me.

R.11: If I do not understand what someone is saying, we are like strangers from different countries who cannot talk to each other.

decisions.choice: force: meaning
decisions.reason: δύναμιν usually means power; of a word or a language it means what it conveys, its meaning.

decisions.choice: foreigner: someone whose language one cannot understand
decisions.reason: βάρβαρος first named a person whose speech sounded to Greeks like meaningless 'bar-bar'. It was used of non-Greeks (Romans 1:14; Colossians 3:11; Acts 28:2), without necessarily meaning savage. Here each of two people is a foreigner to the other, because neither understands.

decisions.choice: in me: in my view, to me
decisions.reason: ἐν ἐμοὶ means 'in my judgment', 'as far as I am concerned'.

decisions.choice: foreigner (L, B); strangers from different countries (R)
decisions.reason: 'Barbarian' now suggests someone uncivilized, which is not the point (m2).

records.source: οὕτως καὶ ὑμεῖς, ἐπεὶ ζηλωταί ἐστε πνευμάτων, πρὸς τὴν οἰκοδομὴν τῆς ἐκκλησίας ζητεῖτε ἵνα περισσεύητε.
records.gloss: So also you, since zealots you are of spirits, for the building up of the church seek that you may abound.
pieces: It is the same with you. Since you are so eager for the workings of the Spirit, aim to have them in abundance for the building up of the church.

L.12: So also you, since you are zealous for spirits, seek to abound for the building up of the church.

R.12: That is true for you too. You really want the Spirit to work through you. So try hard to have plenty of the gifts that help the church grow stronger.

decisions.choice: spirits: the ways the one Spirit is at work in the gifts
alternatives: spirits or spiritual powers in general
spiritual gifts, the same as in verse 1
decisions.reason: πνευμάτων is the plural of 'spirit'. Paul probably means the many ways the one Spirit shows his presence in the gifts (12:7, 'the manifestation of the Spirit'); compare 'the spirits of prophets' in verse 32. Some take it as a looser way of saying 'spiritual gifts'.

decisions.choice: seek to abound for the building up of the church: the church's growth is to be the goal of their eagerness
alternatives: seek to abound in the gifts that build up the church
decisions.reason: πρὸς τὴν οἰκοδομὴν τῆς ἐκκλησίας stands first for emphasis. Paul does not discourage their eagerness; he gives it a goal.

decisions.choice: zealots: eager, keen
decisions.reason: ζηλωταί is the noun related to 'be zealous' in verses 1 and 39; it describes the Corinthians' strong desire, which Paul does not condemn.

decisions.choice: the workings of the Spirit (B); the Spirit to work through you (R)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable say what 'spirits' means here (m1); Literal keeps 'spirits'.

records.source: Διὸ ὁ λαλῶν γλώσσῃ προσευχέσθω ἵνα διερμηνεύῃ.
records.gloss: Therefore the [one] speaking in a tongue let him pray that he may interpret.
pieces: For that reason, anyone who speaks in a tongue should ask God for the power to interpret it as well.

L.13: Therefore let the one speaking in a tongue pray that {{gender:they|he}} may interpret.

R.13: So people who speak in tongues should pray that God will also help them interpret what they say.

decisions.choice: pray that he may interpret: ask God for the gift of interpretation
alternatives: pray in the tongue in such a way that it can then be interpreted
decisions.reason: ἵνα can give the content of the prayer or its purpose. Since interpretation is a gift of the Spirit (12:10), the speaker is told to ask for it.

decisions.choice: therefore: because only a tongue that is interpreted builds up the church
decisions.reason: Διὸ draws the conclusion of verses 5 and 12.

decisions.choice: ask God for the power to interpret it as well (B); pray that God will also help them interpret (R)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable say to whom the prayer is made and what is asked (m1).

records.source: ἐὰν γὰρ προσεύχωμαι γλώσσῃ, τὸ πνεῦμά μου προσεύχεται, ὁ δὲ νοῦς μου ἄκαρπός ἐστιν.
records.gloss: If for I pray in a tongue, the spirit of me prays, the but mind of me unfruitful is.
pieces: When I pray in a tongue, it is my spirit that prays, while my mind bears no fruit.

L.14: For if I pray in a tongue, my spirit prays, but my mind is fruitless.

R.14: When I pray in tongues, my spirit is praying, but my mind is not doing anything useful.

decisions.choice: my spirit: the speaker's own inner self, moved by God's Spirit
alternatives: the Holy Spirit given to me, praying through me
decisions.reason: With 'my', τὸ πνεῦμά μου most naturally means Paul's own spirit, the part of a person that relates to God (2:11; Romans 8:16), here set against his mind. Some read it as the Holy Spirit at work in Paul, since tongues are a gift of the Spirit (12:10). The two are not far apart: in a tongue the Spirit prays through the human spirit without passing through the mind.

decisions.choice: mind: the power of understanding and thinking
decisions.reason: νοῦς is the mind as it understands and reasons (verse 19; 2:16; Romans 12:2).

decisions.choice: without fruit: producing nothing, neither understanding for the speaker nor benefit for others
decisions.reason: ἄκαρπός means barren, yielding nothing. Paul's mind does not understand the words and so has nothing to give the church; verse 19 sets speaking 'with my mind' against this, so that others are taught.

decisions.choice: bears no fruit (B); not doing anything useful (R)
decisions.reason: Balanced keeps the picture; Readable says plainly what it means (m3).

records.source: τί οὖν ἐστιν;
records.gloss: What then is it?
pieces: What follows, then?

decisions.choice: what then is it?: what is the conclusion?
decisions.reason: The short question, used again in verse 26, introduces Paul's conclusion.

decisions.choice: What follows, then? (B); So what will I do? (R)
decisions.reason: Balanced gives the sense of the question; Readable puts it in terms of what Paul will do, which the next sentence answers.

records.source: προσεύξομαι τῷ πνεύματι, προσεύξομαι δὲ καὶ τῷ νοΐ· ψαλῶ τῷ πνεύματι, ψαλῶ δὲ καὶ τῷ νοΐ·
records.gloss: I will pray with the spirit, I will pray but also with the mind; I will sing praise with the spirit, I will sing praise but also with the mind;
pieces: I will pray in the spirit, and I will pray with my mind as well. I will sing praise in the spirit, and I will sing praise with my mind as well.

L.15: I will pray with the spirit, but I will pray also with the mind; I will sing praise with the spirit, but I will sing praise also with the mind.

R.15: I will pray with my spirit, in tongues, and I will also pray with my mind, in words I understand. I will sing with my spirit, in tongues, and I will also sing with my mind, in words I understand.

decisions.choice: with the spirit: with one's own spirit, in a tongue, as in verse 14
decisions.reason: τῷ πνεύματι takes up 'my spirit' of verse 14, and the article points back to it. Praying 'with the spirit' is praying in a tongue; praying 'with the mind' is praying in words one understands. As in verse 14, the human spirit is moved by the Spirit of God.

decisions.choice: sing praise: sing to God
decisions.reason: ψαλῶ is related to the word 'psalm' (verse 26) and means to sing praise to God (Romans 15:9; James 5:13).

decisions.choice: I will: Paul's resolve, set out as a pattern
decisions.reason: The future verbs say what Paul will do. He does not give up praying in tongues, but he joins understanding to it.

decisions.choice: spirit, with a lowercase s
decisions.reason: Lowercase 'spirit' follows the choice in m1, the human spirit; the footnote gives the other reading.

decisions.choice: in tongues; in words I understand
decisions.reason: Readable says what praying with the spirit and with the mind mean (m1).

records.source: ἐπεὶ ἐὰν εὐλογῇς πνεύματι, ὁ ἀναπληρῶν τὸν τόπον τοῦ ἰδιώτου πῶς ἐρεῖ τὸ Ἀμήν ἐπὶ τῇ σῇ εὐχαριστίᾳ;
records.gloss: Otherwise if you bless in spirit, the [one] filling the place of the outsider how will he say the Amen at your thanksgiving?
pieces: Otherwise, if you bless God in the spirit, how will someone who is in the outsider's place say the "Amen" to your prayer of thanks?

L.16: Otherwise, if you bless [God] in [the] spirit, how will the one filling the place of the outsider say the "Amen" at your thanksgiving?

R.16: Suppose you praise God only with your spirit. Someone there who does not understand cannot say "Amen" to agree with your prayer of thanks.

decisions.choice: bless: praise and thank God
decisions.reason: εὐλογῇς, used of people speaking to God, means to praise him and give thanks, as at a meal (10:16). At the end of the sentence the prayer is called a thanksgiving.

decisions.choice: in the spirit: with one's own spirit, in a tongue, as in verses 14-15
decisions.reason: As in verse 15.

decisions.choice: the outsider: someone in the gathering who does not share the gift and cannot understand the tongue, perhaps one not yet fully part of the church
alternatives: an ordinary believer without the gift of tongues or of interpretation
an inquirer, someone interested in the faith but not yet a believer
decisions.reason: ἰδιώτου means a private person, someone without special skill or knowledge (Acts 4:13; 2 Corinthians 11:6). In verses 23-24 the same word stands beside 'unbelievers' but is distinct from them, so it may be someone who attends but has not yet joined the church, or any believer who lacks the gift. Either way the person cannot understand what is said in the tongue.

decisions.choice: filling the place of the outsider: being in the position of one who does not understand
alternatives: sitting in a particular place in the room set aside for outsiders
decisions.reason: ἀναπληρῶν means to fill or occupy. It most likely describes a person's role or situation. Some think of an actual place where visitors sat, but nothing else is known of such seating in the house churches.

decisions.choice: Amen: the word by which hearers agree with a prayer and make it their own
decisions.reason: Ἀμήν is a Hebrew word meaning 'it is true, so be it'. The congregation said it at the end of prayers and blessings (Deuteronomy 27:15-26; Nehemiah 8:6; 2 Corinthians 1:20). No one can say it to a prayer they have not understood.

decisions.choice: outsider
decisions.reason: 'Outsider' says that the person stands outside what is happening, without deciding between the readings in m3.

decisions.choice: only; Someone there who does not understand; to agree with
decisions.reason: Readable names the outsider by the one thing certain about the person, that they do not understand (m3), and says what 'Amen' does (m5).

decisions.choice: prayer of thanks
decisions.reason: 'Thanksgiving' alone may suggest the holiday; the Greek word is a prayer of thanks.

records.source: ἐπειδὴ τί λέγεις οὐκ οἶδεν·
records.gloss: since what you say not he knows;
pieces: That person has no idea what you are saying.

L.16: since [the outsider] does not know what you are saying.

R.16: That person does not know what you are saying.

decisions.choice: since: the reason the outsider cannot say the Amen
decisions.reason: ἐπειδὴ gives the reason for the question before.

decisions.choice: [the outsider] (L); That person (B, R)
decisions.reason: The Greek verb has no stated subject; the levels name the outsider of the sentence before.

records.source: σὺ μὲν γὰρ καλῶς εὐχαριστεῖς, ἀλλ’ ὁ ἕτερος οὐκ οἰκοδομεῖται.
records.gloss: You indeed for well give thanks, but the other not is built up.
pieces: Your thanksgiving may be fine, but it does nothing to build up the other person.

L.17: For you indeed give thanks well, but the other [person] is not built up.

R.17: Your prayer of thanks may be good, but it does not help the other person grow stronger.

decisions.choice: you give thanks well: Paul grants that the prayer itself is good
decisions.reason: μὲν ('indeed') concedes the point before the 'but'. The fault is not in the prayer but in its effect: no one else is helped.

decisions.choice: is built up: is helped to grow, as in verses 3-5
decisions.reason: οἰκοδομεῖται is the verb of verse 4.

decisions.choice: build up (B); grow stronger (R)
decisions.reason: As in verse 3.

records.source: εὐχαριστῶ τῷ θεῷ, πάντων ὑμῶν μᾶλλον γλώσσαις λαλῶ·
records.gloss: I give thanks to the God, than all of you more in tongues I speak;
pieces: I am thankful to God that, more than every one of you, I speak in tongues.

L.18: I thank God, I speak in tongues more than you all;

R.18: I speak in tongues more than any of you, and I thank God for it.

decisions.choice: I thank God: the thanks is for the fact that follows
decisions.reason: The Greek sets the two clauses side by side with no 'that'; the second says what Paul thanks God for.

decisions.choice: Paul does not despise tongues
decisions.reason: Paul has the gift in greater measure than the Corinthians who prize it. What he says about its limits in the gathering (verse 19) comes from one who values it.

decisions.choice: more than all of you: more than any of you
alternatives: in more kinds of tongues than you
decisions.reason: μᾶλλον can mean more often or to a greater degree; the comparison is with every one of them.

decisions.choice: that
decisions.reason: Balanced joins the two clauses with 'that' (m1).

decisions.choice: the fact first, then the thanks
decisions.reason: Readable states what Paul does before thanking God for it.

records.source: ἀλλὰ ἐν ἐκκλησίᾳ θέλω πέντε λόγους τῷ νοΐ μου λαλῆσαι, ἵνα καὶ ἄλλους κατηχήσω, ἢ μυρίους λόγους ἐν γλώσσῃ.
records.gloss: But in church I want five words with the mind of me to speak, so that also others I may instruct, than ten thousand words in a tongue.
pieces: But when the church meets, I would sooner speak five words with my mind, so as to teach others too, than thousands upon thousands of words in a tongue.

L.19: But in church I would rather speak five words with my mind, so that I may also instruct others, than 10,000 words in a tongue.

R.19: But when the church meets together, I would rather say five words that I understand, so that others can learn from them too, than thousands of words in tongues.

decisions.choice: I want ... than: I would prefer
decisions.reason: θέλω followed by ἢ ('than') expresses a preference.

decisions.choice: in church: in the gathering of believers
decisions.reason: As in verse 4, ἐκκλησίᾳ without the article means the assembly when it meets. The contrast with verse 18 suggests that Paul uses tongues elsewhere, in his own prayer.

decisions.choice: instruct: teach
decisions.reason: κατηχήσω means to teach by word of mouth (Romans 2:18; Galatians 6:6).

decisions.choice: ten thousand: a number too great to count
decisions.reason: As in 4:15, μυρίους is the largest Greek number word and stands for a great many; set beside 'five', it makes the contrast as sharp as possible.

decisions.choice: 10,000 (L); thousands upon thousands (B); thousands (R)
decisions.reason: Literal keeps the number, written in figures as in 4:15; Balanced and Readable give its sense (m4). 'Five' is written as a word.

decisions.choice: five words that I understand
decisions.reason: Readable says what speaking with the mind means, as in verse 15.

records.source: Ἀδελφοί, μὴ παιδία γίνεσθε ταῖς φρεσίν, ἀλλὰ τῇ κακίᾳ νηπιάζετε, ταῖς δὲ φρεσὶν τέλειοι γίνεσθε.
records.gloss: Brothers, not children be in the thinking, but in the evil be infants, in the but thinking mature be.
pieces: {{gender:Brothers and sisters|Brothers}}, do not think like children. Be babies where evil is concerned, but in your understanding be grown up.

L.20: {{gender:Brothers and sisters|Brothers}}, do not become children in [your] minds; rather, in wickedness be babies, but in [your] minds become mature.

R.20: {{gender:Brothers and sisters|Brothers}}, stop thinking like little children. When it comes to doing wrong, be like babies who know nothing about it. But in the way you think, be grown-ups.

decisions.choice: minds: thinking, judgment
decisions.reason: φρεσίν is the mind as it thinks and judges; the word occurs only here in the New Testament.

decisions.choice: children, babies, mature: stages of growing up
decisions.reason: παιδία are young children, νηπιάζετε means to be like an infant, and τέλειοι are those who are grown, the mature (2:6). Paul wants them innocent of evil but adult in judgment, the judgment their love of tongues lacked. Compare 3:1-2 and 13:11.

decisions.choice: wickedness: evil, malice
decisions.reason: κακίᾳ is badness of every kind, including ill will toward others (5:8).

decisions.choice: grown up (B); grown-ups (R)
decisions.reason: Plain words keep the picture of growing up; Literal keeps 'mature', as in 2:6.

records.heading: Tongues, prophecy and outsiders

records.source: ἐν τῷ νόμῳ γέγραπται ὅτι Ἐν ἑτερογλώσσοις καὶ ἐν χείλεσιν ἑτέρων λαλήσω τῷ λαῷ τούτῳ, καὶ οὐδ’ οὕτως εἰσακούσονταί μου, λέγει κύριος.
records.gloss: In the law it has been written that, By [people of] other tongues and by lips of others I will speak to the people this, and not even thus will they listen to me, says [the] Lord.
pieces: It is written in the law: "Through those who speak other tongues, and through the lips of strangers, I will speak to this people; and not even then will they heed {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}}, says the Lord."

L.21: In the law it is written, "By [people of] other tongues and by [the] lips of others I will speak to this people, and not even so will they listen to {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}}, says [the] Lord."

R.21: In the law, God's written word, the Lord says, "I will speak to this people through foreigners who speak other tongues. But they will still not listen to {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}}."

decisions.choice: a quotation of Isaiah 28:11-12
decisions.reason: Paul quotes Isaiah 28:11-12 freely: his wording follows neither the Hebrew nor the Greek Old Testament closely, and he has God speak in the first person ('I will speak'). In Isaiah the LORD warns the people of Jerusalem, who mocked the prophet's plain message, that he will speak to them through the foreign speech of Assyrian invaders, and even then they will not listen. Reviewers should check the wording against both.

decisions.choice: the law: the Scriptures as a whole
decisions.reason: Isaiah is not one of the books of Moses, but νόμῳ could stand for the whole of Scripture (John 10:34, quoting a psalm; Romans 3:10-19, where words from the Psalms and Isaiah are called what 'the law says').

decisions.choice: says the Lord: the God of Israel speaks; the divine name stands behind 'Lord'
decisions.reason: These words are not in Isaiah 28:11-12. Paul adds the formula with which the prophets mark God's own speech, as in Isaiah 1:11 and often. In the Hebrew prophets that formula uses the divine name, the LORD; the Greek Old Testament and Paul have κύριος.

decisions.choice: other tongues, lips of others: foreign languages
decisions.reason: ἑτερογλώσσοις means people of another language. In Isaiah the foreign speech is a sign of judgment on those who would not listen to the plain word; Paul draws on that in verse 22.

decisions.choice: Lord
decisions.reason: As in 3:20: Paul's Greek has the word for 'Lord', so English writes 'Lord', and m3 notes the divine name behind it.

decisions.choice: God's written word
decisions.reason: Readable explains that 'the law' here means the Scriptures (m2).

decisions.choice: {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}}
decisions.reason: God speaks of himself, so the pronoun takes the deity_pronoun setting.

decisions.choice: foreigners who speak other tongues
decisions.reason: Readable keeps 'tongues', the word of this chapter, and says that the speakers are foreigners, as in Isaiah (m4).

records.source: ὥστε αἱ γλῶσσαι εἰς σημεῖόν εἰσιν οὐ τοῖς πιστεύουσιν ἀλλὰ τοῖς ἀπίστοις, ἡ δὲ προφητεία οὐ τοῖς ἀπίστοις ἀλλὰ τοῖς πιστεύουσιν.
records.gloss: So that the tongues for a sign are not to the believing but to the unbelieving, the but prophecy not to the unbelieving but to the believing.
pieces: So tongues serve as a sign, but the sign is for unbelievers, not for those who believe. Prophecy, on the other hand, is for those who believe, not for unbelievers.

L.22: So then tongues are for a sign, not to those who believe but to unbelievers; but prophecy [is] not to unbelievers but to those who believe.

R.22: So speaking in tongues is a sign for people who do not believe, not for believers. But prophecy is for believers, not for people who do not believe.

decisions.choice: so then: a conclusion drawn from the quotation
decisions.reason: ὥστε draws the lesson of Isaiah 28:11-12 (verse 21).

decisions.choice: a sign for unbelievers: a sign of judgment, which leaves them in their unbelief, as the foreign speech did in Isaiah
alternatives: a sign meant to lead unbelievers to faith, as at Pentecost (Acts 2:5-12)
a sign that shows who the unbelievers are, because they cannot understand
Paul quotes a view held in Corinth and corrects it in verses 23-25
decisions.reason: In Isaiah the strange speech of foreigners came on a people who refused to listen, and 'even then they will not listen' (verse 21). Verse 23 bears this out: unbelievers who hear tongues say 'you are raving' and do not come to faith. The sentence is hard, because verses 24-25 show prophecy at work on an unbeliever, which seems to reverse what this verse says of prophecy.

decisions.choice: prophecy is for believers: it serves those who believe; whether it is also called a sign is left open
alternatives: prophecy is a sign for believers, of God's presence among them
decisions.reason: The second half has no verb and does not repeat 'sign'. It may mean simply that prophecy is meant for believers, or that it is a sign for them. Verses 24-25 show that it also reaches an unbeliever who hears it.

decisions.choice: unbelievers: people who do not believe in Christ
decisions.reason: ἀπίστοις means people who do not believe, as in 6:6 and 7:12-15; in verses 23-24 they stand beside outsiders.

decisions.choice: the group each gift is for comes first
alternatives: not for believers but for unbelievers
decisions.reason: Balanced names first the group each gift is for, which makes the contrast easier to follow.

records.source: ἐὰν οὖν συνέλθῃ ἡ ἐκκλησία ὅλη ἐπὶ τὸ αὐτὸ καὶ πάντες λαλῶσιν γλώσσαις, εἰσέλθωσιν δὲ ἰδιῶται ἢ ἄπιστοι, οὐκ ἐροῦσιν ὅτι μαίνεσθε;
records.gloss: If therefore comes together the church whole at the same [place] and all speak in tongues, come in but outsiders or unbelievers, not will they say that you are raving?
pieces: Picture the whole church gathered in one place, with everyone speaking in tongues. If outsiders or unbelievers walk in, will they not say you have gone mad?

L.23: So if the whole church comes together in the same [place] and all speak in tongues, and outsiders or unbelievers come in, will they not say, "You are raving"?

R.23: Imagine that the whole church meets together and everyone speaks in tongues. Then some people come in who do not understand, or who do not believe. They will say you have lost your minds!

decisions.choice: raving: out of one's mind, in a frenzy
decisions.reason: μαίνεσθε; means to be mad. Outsiders would hear something like the frenzy of some pagan cults (12:2), not the voice of God.

decisions.choice: outsiders or unbelievers: two groups, those who do not understand because they are new or lack the gift, and those who do not believe
alternatives: one group described in two ways
decisions.reason: As in verse 16, ἰδιῶται means a person who stands outside, here set beside ἄπιστοι. It may be someone interested in the faith but not yet a believer, or a believer who does not understand tongues; verse 24 has the same pair in the singular.

decisions.choice: the whole church in the same place: all the believers of the city meeting together
decisions.reason: Believers in Corinth usually met in houses (16:19). Romans 16:23, written from Corinth, calls Gaius host 'to the whole church'. Paul imagines all of them gathered and visitors coming in.

decisions.choice: will they not say?: they certainly will
decisions.reason: The question expects the answer yes.

decisions.choice: They will say you have lost your minds!
alternatives: Will they not say you are raving?
decisions.reason: Readable gives the answer the question expects (m4).

decisions.choice: people ... who do not understand
decisions.reason: As in verse 16, Readable names the outsider by the one thing certain, that such a person does not understand.

records.source: ἐὰν δὲ πάντες προφητεύωσιν, εἰσέλθῃ δέ τις ἄπιστος ἢ ἰδιώτης, ἐλέγχεται ὑπὸ πάντων, ἀνακρίνεται ὑπὸ πάντων, τὰ κρυπτὰ τῆς καρδίας αὐτοῦ φανερὰ γίνεται, καὶ οὕτως πεσὼν ἐπὶ πρόσωπον προσκυνήσει τῷ θεῷ, ἀπαγγέλλων ὅτι Ὄντως ὁ θεὸς ἐν ὑμῖν ἐστιν.
records.gloss: If but all prophesy, comes in but some unbeliever or outsider, he is convicted by all, he is examined by all, \v 25 the secrets of the heart of him manifest become, and thus having fallen on face he will worship the God, declaring that, Really the God among you is.
pieces: But if everyone is prophesying, and some unbeliever or outsider comes in, {{gender:they are|he is}} convicted by what all are saying and examined by what all are saying.
The secrets of {{gender:their|his}} heart come into the open, and so {{gender:they|he}} will fall face down and worship God, declaring, "God really is among you!"

L.24: But if all prophesy, and some unbeliever or outsider comes in, {{gender:they are|he is}} convicted by all, {{gender:they are|he is}} examined by all;
L.25: the secrets of {{gender:their|his}} heart become manifest, and so, falling on [the] face, {{gender:they|he}} will worship God, declaring, "Truly God is among you."

R.24: But suppose everyone is prophesying when an unbeliever or someone who does not understand comes in. What everyone says will show {{gender:them|him}} {{gender:their|his}} sin and make {{gender:them|him}} look hard at {{gender:their|his}} life.
R.25: The secret things in {{gender:their|his}} heart will be brought out into the open. Then {{gender:they|he}} will bow down with {{gender:their|his}} face to the ground and worship God. {{gender:They|He}} will say, "God is truly here among you!"

decisions.choice: convicted: shown to be in the wrong, brought to see one's sin
decisions.reason: ἐλέγχεται means to expose, to prove someone guilty, and so to bring them to conviction (John 16:8; Ephesians 5:13).

decisions.choice: examined: searched and assessed
decisions.reason: ἀνακρίνεται is the verb for examining or judging in 2:14-15 and 4:3-4. What the prophets say probes the hearer's life.

decisions.choice: the secrets of the heart become manifest: God shows the hearer what lies hidden within
decisions.reason: Only God knows the secrets of the heart (4:5; Psalm 44:22). When prophecy lays them bare, the hearer knows that God is present. The stress is on what the hearer comes to see, not on prophets telling others' secrets.

decisions.choice: falling on the face: bowing to the ground, the posture of worship
decisions.reason: To fall on one's face was to bow fully to the ground before God or a king (Genesis 17:3; Matthew 2:11, where the Magi fall down and worship).

decisions.choice: God is really among you: words like Isaiah 45:14 and Zechariah 8:23
decisions.reason: In Isaiah 45:14 foreigners come and bow down to Israel, saying 'Surely God is among you'; in Zechariah 8:23 people of the nations say 'God is with you'. The outsider's confession fulfills what the prophets expected of the nations.

decisions.choice: among you: present in your gathering
alternatives: in you, within each of you
decisions.reason: ἐν ὑμῖν can mean 'among you' or 'in you'. The outsider speaks of what is seen in the gathered church.

decisions.choice: {{gender:they|he}} and the related pronouns
decisions.reason: The person may be a man or a woman, so the gender setting applies; the Greek uses masculine forms for any person.

decisions.choice: show them their sin; make them look hard at their life
decisions.reason: Readable says in plain words what being convicted and examined mean (m1, m2).

records.source: Τί οὖν ἐστιν, ἀδελφοί;
records.gloss: What then is it, brothers?
pieces: What follows, then, {{gender:brothers and sisters|brothers}}?

R.26: So what does all this mean for you, {{gender:brothers and sisters|brothers}}?

decisions.choice: what then is it?: what follows?
decisions.reason: As in verse 15, the question leads to Paul's practical conclusion for their gatherings.

decisions.choice: What follows, then? (B); what does all this mean for you? (R)
decisions.reason: As in verse 15, Balanced and Readable give the sense of the question.

records.heading: Order when the church meets

records.source: ὅταν συνέρχησθε, ἕκαστος ψαλμὸν ἔχει, διδαχὴν ἔχει, ἀποκάλυψιν ἔχει, γλῶσσαν ἔχει, ἑρμηνείαν ἔχει· πάντα πρὸς οἰκοδομὴν γινέσθω.
records.gloss: Whenever you come together, each a psalm has, a teaching has, a revelation has, a tongue has, an interpretation has; all things for building up let be done.
pieces: Whenever you gather, each of you has something: a psalm, a teaching, a revelation, a tongue, an interpretation. Everything should be done to build up the church.

L.26: Whenever you come together, each one has a psalm, has a teaching, has a revelation, has a tongue, has an interpretation; let all things be done for building up.

R.26: When you meet together, each of you has something to share. One person has a song of praise. Another has a teaching, or a revelation from God. Another speaks in a tongue, and another interprets it. Everything you do must help the church grow stronger.

decisions.choice: each has: each person brings something, one this and another that
alternatives: every person has every one of these
decisions.reason: ἕκαστος with the repeated verb describes what happens when they meet: one has a psalm, another a teaching, and so on. Paul does not say that every believer has all five.

decisions.choice: a description of their gatherings, which Paul accepts and then regulates
alternatives: a mild rebuke: everyone wants a turn at once
decisions.reason: The sentence describes what each brings without blame, and the command that follows sets the rule for it. Some hear a complaint that everyone brings something and all want to speak, which verses 27-33 then put in order.

decisions.choice: psalm: a song of praise to God, perhaps a psalm of Scripture or a new song
decisions.reason: ψαλμὸν can be a psalm from the Old Testament or a song composed in the same manner (verse 15; Ephesians 5:19; Colossians 3:16).

decisions.choice: teaching, revelation, tongue, interpretation: the kinds of speech named in verse 6 and the gifts of 12:10
decisions.reason: ἀποκάλυψιν is a revelation given by God to a prophet (verse 30); γλῶσσαν and ἑρμηνείαν are a tongue and its interpretation.

decisions.choice: let all things be done for building up: the rule for every contribution
decisions.reason: The test of verses 3-5, 12 and 17 now governs everything done when the church meets.

decisions.choice: a song of praise
decisions.reason: Readable says what a psalm is (m3).

decisions.choice: the church
decisions.reason: The Greek says only 'for building up'; the church is what is built up, as in verses 4, 5 and 12.

records.source: εἴτε γλώσσῃ τις λαλεῖ, κατὰ δύο ἢ τὸ πλεῖστον τρεῖς, καὶ ἀνὰ μέρος, καὶ εἷς διερμηνευέτω·
records.gloss: Whether in a tongue anyone speaks, by two or the most three, and in turn, and one let interpret;
pieces: As for speaking in a tongue, let it be done by two people, or by three at the most, each taking a turn, and let one person interpret.

L.27: If anyone speaks in a tongue, [let it be] by two, or at the most three, and in turn; and one is to interpret.

R.27: If people speak in tongues, only two or three should do it at a meeting. They should take turns, and one person must interpret what they say.

decisions.choice: two or at the most three: at each gathering
alternatives: two or three at a time
decisions.reason: κατὰ δύο distributes: two, or three, on each occasion. The next words, 'in turn', rule out speaking at the same time.

decisions.choice: in turn: one after another
decisions.reason: ἀνὰ μέρος means by turns, each in their part.

decisions.choice: one: one person interprets, perhaps the same person for all who speak
decisions.reason: εἷς is the number one. It may simply mean 'someone', or that one person should interpret, so that interpreters do not compete. Verses 5 and 13 show that the speaker may also be the interpreter.

decisions.choice: [let it be] (L); at a meeting (R)
decisions.reason: The Greek has no verb for the numbers; Literal supplies one, and Readable says that the limit is for each gathering (m1).

records.source: ἐὰν δὲ μὴ ᾖ διερμηνευτής, σιγάτω ἐν ἐκκλησίᾳ, ἑαυτῷ δὲ λαλείτω καὶ τῷ θεῷ.
records.gloss: If but not there is an interpreter, let him be silent in church, to himself and let him speak and to the God.
pieces: If there is no one to interpret, the speaker should keep silent in the church, speaking only to {{gender:themselves|himself}} and to God.

L.28: But if there is no interpreter, let {{gender:them|him}} be silent in church, and let {{gender:them|him}} speak to {{gender:themselves|himself}} and to God.

R.28: If no one is there who can interpret, those who speak in tongues should be silent during the meeting. They can speak quietly to themselves and to God.

decisions.choice: be silent: stop speaking aloud in the gathering, in the situation described
decisions.reason: σιγάτω means to be or become silent. Paul uses the same verb for the speaker in tongues here, for a prophet in verse 30, and for women in verse 34. Here the silence applies only when no interpreter is present.

decisions.choice: speak to oneself and to God: pray in the tongue quietly, without addressing the church
alternatives: pray in tongues elsewhere, in private
decisions.reason: ἑαυτῷ ('to himself') sets this speech against speech to the church. Paul does not say whether it is quiet prayer during the meeting or prayer elsewhere; either way it is speech to God, as in verse 2.

decisions.choice: an interpreter: someone with the gift of interpretation, who may be the speaker (verse 13)
decisions.reason: διερμηνευτής is the one who interprets, a gift named in 12:10.

decisions.choice: be silent (L, R); keep silent (B)
decisions.reason: The same English for the same verb in verses 28, 30 and 34, so that readers can compare them (m1).

decisions.choice: quietly
decisions.reason: Readable follows m2: the speaking is not addressed to the gathering.

records.source: προφῆται δὲ δύο ἢ τρεῖς λαλείτωσαν, καὶ οἱ ἄλλοι διακρινέτωσαν·
records.gloss: Prophets and two or three let speak, and the others let weigh;
pieces: As for prophets, let two or three speak, and let the others weigh their words.

L.29: And let two or three prophets speak, and let the others weigh [what is said].

R.29: Two or three prophets may speak at a meeting. The others should think carefully about what they say, to see whether it comes from God.

decisions.choice: weigh: assess what is said, to tell what comes from God
decisions.reason: διακρινέτωσαν is related to the gift of 'distinguishing of spirits' (12:10): telling apart what is from God's Spirit and what is not. Prophecy was to be tested, not simply accepted (1 Thessalonians 5:20-21; 1 John 4:1).

decisions.choice: the others: the other prophets present
decisions.reason: οἱ ἄλλοι most naturally means the rest of the group just named, the prophets. But testing prophecy is elsewhere the work of the whole church (1 Thessalonians 5:20-21), and all believers have the Spirit (12:3, 13), so some take it of everyone present.

decisions.choice: weigh
decisions.reason: 'Weigh' means to assess, not to condemn (m1).

decisions.choice: [what is said] (L); to see whether it comes from God (R)
decisions.reason: Literal supplies the object; Readable says what weighing is for (m1).

records.source: ἐὰν δὲ ἄλλῳ ἀποκαλυφθῇ καθημένῳ, ὁ πρῶτος σιγάτω.
records.gloss: If but to another it is revealed sitting, the first let be silent.
pieces: And if something is revealed to another person who is sitting there, the first speaker should keep silent.

L.30: But if [something] is revealed to another who is sitting [there], let the first be silent.

R.30: If God shows something to another person who is sitting there, the first prophet should be silent and let that person speak.

decisions.choice: is revealed: God gives a revelation
decisions.reason: ἀποκαλυφθῇ is passive, with God as the one who reveals (2:10). This is the 'revelation' of verses 6 and 26, given to a prophet.

decisions.choice: sitting: the hearers sat while the one speaking stood
decisions.reason: A speaker could stand to address a gathering (Acts 13:16); here the others are seated. The word marks the person as one of the hearers.

decisions.choice: be silent: the first prophet stops, to let the other speak
decisions.reason: The same verb as in verses 28 and 34. Here it means giving way, as verse 31 explains: all can prophesy in turn.

decisions.choice: God shows; and let that person speak
decisions.reason: Readable names God as the one who reveals (m1) and says why the first prophet is silent (m3).

decisions.choice: be silent (L, R); keep silent (B)
decisions.reason: As in verse 28.

records.source: δύνασθε γὰρ καθ’ ἕνα πάντες προφητεύειν, ἵνα πάντες μανθάνωσιν καὶ πάντες παρακαλῶνται καὶ πνεύματα προφητῶν προφήταις ὑποτάσσεται, οὐ γάρ ἐστιν ἀκαταστασίας ὁ θεὸς ἀλλὰ εἰρήνης, ὡς ἐν πάσαις ταῖς ἐκκλησίαις τῶν ἁγίων.
records.gloss: You are able for one by one all to prophesy, so that all may learn and all may be encouraged \v 32 and spirits of prophets to prophets are subject, \v 33 not for is of disorder the God but of peace, as in all the churches of the holy ones.
pieces: You can all prophesy, each in turn, so that all of you learn and all of you are encouraged.
Prophets have their own spirits under their control.
God is the God of peace, not of disorder, as is true in all the churches of God's holy people.

L.31: For you are all able to prophesy one at a time, so that all may learn and all may be encouraged;
L.32: and prophets' spirits are subject to prophets,
L.33: for God is [the God] not of disorder but of peace, as in all the churches of the holy ones.

R.31: All of you can prophesy, one at a time, so that everyone can learn and everyone can be encouraged.
R.32: Prophets can control themselves when they prophesy.
R.33: God does not cause confusion. He brings peace. That is true in all the churches of God's people.

decisions.choice: you can all prophesy one by one: there is room for every prophet to speak, in turn
decisions.reason: ἕνα with the preposition before it means one at a time. πάντες probably means all who have the gift of prophecy, not every believer (12:29: not all are prophets).

decisions.choice: be encouraged: be urged on and strengthened
decisions.reason: παρακαλῶνται is the verb related to 'encouragement' in verse 3.

decisions.choice: the spirits of prophets are subject to prophets: prophets can control their own inspired speech, and so can wait their turn
alternatives: what one prophet says is subject to the assessment of the other prophets (verse 29)
decisions.reason: πνεύματα προφητῶν are the prophets' own spirits as God's Spirit moves them, as with 'my spirit' in verse 14. Prophecy does not seize a person against their will, so a prophet can stop to let another speak (verse 30). Others read the words with verse 29: what one prophet says is subject to the others who weigh it.

decisions.choice: God is not a God of disorder but of peace: the way the church meets should reflect who God is
decisions.reason: ἀκαταστασίας is disorder, unrest (2 Corinthians 12:20). God is the God of peace (Romans 15:33; 16:20; Philippians 4:9), and a gathering where all speak at once does not show him.

decisions.choice: as in all the churches of the holy ones: belongs with what comes before, closing Paul's teaching on orderly speaking
alternatives: begins the next sentence: 'As in all the churches of the holy ones, let the women be silent in the churches'
decisions.reason: Ancient manuscripts have little punctuation, so where the phrase belongs is an editorial judgment. The SBLGNT puts a comma before it and a full stop after it, so that it ends Paul's teaching on orderly speaking; Paul ends other instructions with an appeal to what all the churches do (4:17; 7:17; 11:16). Others join it to verse 34, which would then begin 'As in all the churches'; but that sentence goes on to say 'in the churches' again.

decisions.choice: the holy ones: God's people, set apart for him
decisions.reason: As in 1:2 and 6:1-2, ἁγίων are all believers, not a special class.

decisions.choice: Prophets have their own spirits under their control (B); Prophets can control themselves when they prophesy (R)
alternatives: the spirits of prophets are subject to prophets
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable follow m3. Literal keeps the Greek wording, which can be read either way.

decisions.choice: God's holy people (B); God's people (R)
decisions.reason: As in Philippians and Colossians; Literal says 'the holy ones'.

decisions.choice: God is the God of peace, not of disorder
alternatives: God is not a God of disorder but of peace
decisions.reason: Balanced puts the positive statement first.

records.source: Αἱ γυναῖκες ἐν ταῖς ἐκκλησίαις σιγάτωσαν, οὐ γὰρ ἐπιτρέπεται αὐταῖς λαλεῖν· ἀλλὰ ὑποτασσέσθωσαν, καθὼς καὶ ὁ νόμος λέγει.
records.gloss: The women in the churches let be silent, not for it is permitted to them to speak; but let them be subject, just as also the law says.
pieces: In the churches the women are to keep silent. They are not permitted to speak; instead they are to be subject, as the law also says.

L.34: Let the women be silent in the churches, for it is not permitted for them to speak; but let them be subject, just as the law also says.

R.34: In the church meetings the women must be silent. They are not allowed to speak. Instead, they must be submissive, as the law also says.

decisions.choice: verses 34-35 stand here, after verse 33, as the SBLGNT prints them
alternatives: the verses stand after verse 40, as in some manuscripts
the verses were not written by Paul but added to the letter later
decisions.reason: Verses 34-35 are found in every known manuscript of the letter, but not all in the same place: some manuscripts, Greek and Latin witnesses of the so-called Western text, place them after verse 40, at the end of the chapter. Because of this displacement, some scholars think the verses began as a note in the margin that copyists later put into the text at two different points, and so question whether Paul wrote them; others hold that he did and that the verses were moved by copyists. The SBLGNT prints them here, and this translation follows it. Reviewers must check the evidence against the SBLGNT apparatus.

decisions.choice: the women: women in the gathering, in general
alternatives: wives: married women, whose husbands are mentioned in verse 35
decisions.reason: γυναῖκες means both 'women' and 'wives'. As in 11:3-16, the general sense is chosen, since the sentence speaks of women in the churches. But verse 35 tells them to ask 'their own husbands', so married women are at least the main ones in view, and some read 'wives' throughout. In that world most adult women were married.

decisions.choice: a particular kind of speaking that disturbed the gathering, most likely asking questions aloud during the meeting, not every kind of speech
alternatives: speaking in the weighing of prophecies (verse 29), perhaps judging what one's own husband had prophesied
a saying of some in Corinth, which Paul quotes in verses 34-35 and rejects in verse 36
a general rule that women are not to speak at all when the church meets
decisions.reason: In 11:5 Paul takes it for granted that women pray and prophesy aloud when the church meets, and tells them only how to be dressed when they do. So the silence here is probably not total. The context is about order: the speaker in tongues is to be silent when there is no interpreter (verse 28), and a prophet when another receives a revelation (verse 30). Verse 35 speaks of wanting to learn and of asking at home, which points to questions. Some connect the verse with the weighing of prophecies just mentioned (verse 29). Some read verses 34-35 as a Corinthian view that Paul quotes and answers in verse 36, though nothing in the Greek marks them as a quotation. Others take them as a general rule for worship. λαλεῖν is the ordinary verb 'speak', used throughout the chapter for tongues and prophecy as well as for ordinary talk, so the word itself does not decide.

decisions.choice: the law: Paul does not say which law, and what is meant is not clear
alternatives: the account of creation in Genesis 2, as in 11:8-9
Genesis 3:16, where the husband rules over the wife
the teaching of the Old Testament in general
Jewish or Roman law and custom of the time
decisions.reason: No passage of the Old Testament commands women to be silent. 'As the law also says' appeals to νόμος, which Paul uses of the law of Moses and, in verse 21, of the Scriptures as a whole. He may mean the order of creation (11:8-9), or Genesis 3:16, or the general teaching of Scripture; others think of Jewish tradition or of the customs of the time. Paul does not say.

decisions.choice: be subject: take their place in an order under another; to whom is not stated
alternatives: subject to the order of the gathering, as the spirits of prophets are subject to prophets (verse 32)
decisions.reason: ὑποτασσέσθωσαν is the same verb as in verse 32. It means to put oneself under, to take one's place in an order; the Greek names no one to whom the women are subject. Verse 35 suggests their husbands; verse 32 suggests the orderly conduct of the meeting.

decisions.choice: it is not permitted: the practice of the churches does not allow it
decisions.reason: ἐπιτρέπεται is passive and does not say who forbids. The appeal to 'all the churches' just before (verse 33) and to 'the law' points to a practice held in common.

decisions.choice: be silent (L, R); keep silent (B)
decisions.reason: The same English as for the same verb in verses 28 and 30, so that readers can compare them.

decisions.choice: be subject (L, B); be submissive (R)
decisions.reason: 'Be subject' is the same English as in verse 32, so the link is visible; Readable says 'submissive', a plainer word for the same thing. No level says to whom (m5).

decisions.choice: women
decisions.reason: As in 11:3-16 (m2); the footnote gives 'wives'.

decisions.choice: In the church meetings
decisions.reason: Readable makes clear that 'the churches' are the gatherings of believers, not buildings.

records.source: εἰ δέ τι μαθεῖν θέλουσιν, ἐν οἴκῳ τοὺς ἰδίους ἄνδρας ἐπερωτάτωσαν, αἰσχρὸν γάρ ἐστιν γυναικὶ λαλεῖν ἐν ἐκκλησίᾳ.
records.gloss: If but something to learn they want, at home the own husbands let them ask, shameful for it is for a woman to speak in church.
pieces: If there is something they wish to learn, they are to put their questions to their own husbands at home. It is shameful for a woman to speak when the church meets.

L.35: And if they want to learn something, let them question their own husbands at home; for it is shameful for a woman to speak in church.

R.35: If they want to learn about something, they should ask their own husbands when they are at home. It is shameful for a woman to speak in a church meeting.

decisions.choice: the verse stands here, with verse 34, as the SBLGNT prints it
alternatives: the verse stands after verse 40, as in some manuscripts
decisions.reason: This verse moves with verse 34: the manuscripts that place verse 34 after verse 40 place this verse there too. See the text decision on verse 34. Reviewers must check the evidence against the SBLGNT apparatus.

decisions.choice: their own husbands: the women in view are, at least mainly, married
decisions.reason: τοὺς ἰδίους ἄνδρας is 'their own men', which here means husbands, as in 7:2 ('her own husband'). Paul does not say what unmarried women or widows, who had no husband to ask, should do (7:8, 34).

decisions.choice: if they want to learn: the speaking in view is tied to learning and asking
decisions.reason: Paul assumes that the women want to learn and gives them a place to do it. This is one reason the speaking forbidden in verse 34 is read as asking questions (decision m3 there).

decisions.choice: shameful: bringing dishonor in the eyes of others
decisions.reason: αἰσχρὸν is the word used in 11:6 of a woman's cropped or shaved head. In the Greek and Roman world it was widely thought improper for a married woman to speak with men outside her family in public; Paul appeals to that sense of shame.

decisions.choice: a woman: the same word as 'the women' in verse 34
decisions.reason: As in verse 34 (m2 there).

decisions.choice: when the church meets (B); in a church meeting (R)
decisions.reason: ἐν ἐκκλησίᾳ has no article: the church as it meets, not a building. Literal keeps 'in church'.

decisions.choice: put their questions to
decisions.reason: Balanced keeps the sense of the verb, which is asking questions.

records.source: ἢ ἀφ’ ὑμῶν ὁ λόγος τοῦ θεοῦ ἐξῆλθεν, ἢ εἰς ὑμᾶς μόνους κατήντησεν;
records.gloss: Or from you the word of the God went out, or to you alone did it reach?
pieces: Or did God's word go out from you? Has it come to you and no one else?

L.36: Or did the word of God go out from you, or did it reach you alone?

R.36: Do you think God's message began with you? Do you think you are the only people who have received it?

decisions.choice: rhetorical questions that expect the answer no
decisions.reason: The two questions, each opened by ἢ ('or'), mean that the word of God did not start in Corinth, and that the Corinthians are not its only receivers. They should follow what all the churches do (verse 33; 11:16).

decisions.choice: you alone: the whole church at Corinth is addressed
alternatives: Paul answers a Corinthian saying in verses 34-35, as if to say: 'What! Did the word of God come from you?'
decisions.reason: μόνους is masculine plural, the form used for a mixed group, so Paul speaks to the church as a whole, and probably to all who think they may set their own rules (verse 37). Those who read verses 34-35 as a Corinthian saying take ἢ as an exclamation rejecting it; the word can introduce such a reply, but nothing marks the verses before it as a quotation.

decisions.choice: the word of God: the message of the gospel
decisions.reason: ὁ λόγος τοῦ θεοῦ is the gospel God has spoken, which reached Corinth through Paul (Acts 18:1-11; 2 Corinthians 10:14).

decisions.choice: Do you think
decisions.reason: Readable makes clear that the questions challenge what the Corinthians assume (m1).

decisions.choice: God's message
decisions.reason: Readable uses a plainer word for the same thing (m3).

records.source: Εἴ τις δοκεῖ προφήτης εἶναι ἢ πνευματικός, ἐπιγινωσκέτω ἃ γράφω ὑμῖν ὅτι κυρίου ἐστὶν·
records.gloss: If anyone thinks a prophet to be or spiritual, let him recognize [the things] which I write to you, that of [the] Lord it is;
pieces: If anyone thinks {{gender:they are|he is}} a prophet or spiritual, {{gender:they|he}} should recognize that what I am writing to you comes from the Lord.

L.37: If anyone thinks {{gender:they are|he is}} a prophet or spiritual, let {{gender:them|him}} recognize that the things I write to you are of [the] Lord.

R.37: Some of you may think you are prophets or have special gifts from the Spirit. If so, you should see that what I am writing to you comes from the Lord.

decisions.choice: what Paul writes 'is of the Lord', as the SBLGNT prints it
alternatives: 'is a command of the Lord', as many manuscripts read
'are commands of the Lord', as other manuscripts read
decisions.reason: Many manuscripts add the word for 'command' after 'of the Lord', some in the singular and some in the plural. The SBLGNT follows manuscripts that lack it, and the different forms of the addition suggest that copyists supplied it to complete the phrase. The sense is much the same: what Paul writes carries the Lord's authority. Reviewers must check the evidence against the SBLGNT apparatus.

decisions.choice: spiritual: a person of the Spirit, gifted by the Spirit
decisions.reason: πνευματικός is the word of 2:15 and 3:1. Some in Corinth seem to have claimed to be spiritual because of their gifts; Paul says that someone truly spiritual will recognize his instruction.

decisions.choice: thinks: considers oneself, perhaps claims to be
decisions.reason: δοκεῖ means to think or seem; here it is what people think of themselves (3:18; 8:2).

decisions.choice: the Lord: Jesus Christ
decisions.reason: As often in this letter, κυρίου alone means the Lord Jesus (7:10, 25).

decisions.choice: have special gifts from the Spirit
decisions.reason: Readable says what being spiritual means here (m2).

decisions.choice: Some of you may think you are
decisions.reason: Readable speaks directly to the readers, as the next words do ('what I am writing to you').

records.source: εἰ δέ τις ἀγνοεῖ, ἀγνοεῖται.
records.gloss: If but anyone does not recognize, he is not recognized.
pieces: Anyone who refuses to recognize this is not recognized either.

L.38: But if anyone does not recognize [this], {{gender:they are|he is}} not recognized.

R.38: If anyone refuses to recognize this, God does not recognize that person either.

decisions.choice: is not recognized: a statement, as the SBLGNT prints it
alternatives: 'let him not recognize it', a command, as other manuscripts read
decisions.reason: Some manuscripts have a command form of the same verb, 'let him be ignorant', meaning that Paul will leave such a person to their ignorance. Others, which the SBLGNT follows, have the passive statement. The two forms differ by only a few letters. Reviewers must check the evidence against the SBLGNT apparatus.

decisions.choice: is not recognized: by God
alternatives: is not to be recognized by the church as a prophet or spiritual person
decisions.reason: ἀγνοεῖται is passive, and Paul often leaves God unnamed as the one who acts. In 8:3 the one who loves God is known by him; here the one who does not acknowledge the Lord's word is not acknowledged. Some take it as a word to the church: do not accept such a person's claim to be a prophet.

decisions.choice: a play on one verb: whoever does not recognize is not recognized
decisions.reason: ἀγνοεῖ and ἀγνοεῖται are the active and passive of the same verb, which means not to know or not to acknowledge; the consequence matches the fault, and it answers 'let him recognize' in verse 37.

decisions.choice: God does not recognize that person
decisions.reason: Readable names God as the one who does not recognize (m2); since that is uncertain, it is marked for reviewers.

decisions.choice: refuses to recognize
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable show that the failure is a refusal, the opposite of 'recognize' in verse 37 (m3).

records.source: ὥστε, ἀδελφοί μου, ζηλοῦτε τὸ προφητεύειν, καὶ τὸ λαλεῖν μὴ κωλύετε γλώσσαις·
records.gloss: So then, brothers of me, be zealous for the to prophesy, and the to speak do not forbid in tongues;
pieces: So then, my {{gender:brothers and sisters|brothers}}, set your hearts on prophesying, and do not stop anyone from speaking in tongues.

L.39: So then, my {{gender:brothers and sisters|brothers}}, be zealous to prophesy, and do not forbid speaking in tongues.

R.39: So, my {{gender:brothers and sisters|brothers}}, try hard to prophesy. And do not stop people from speaking in tongues.

decisions.choice: so then: the conclusion of the chapter
decisions.reason: ὥστε sums up chapters 12-14 in two commands.

decisions.choice: be zealous for: seek eagerly, as in 12:31 and 14:1
decisions.reason: ζηλοῦτε is the verb of 12:31 and 14:1.

decisions.choice: do not forbid speaking in tongues: tongues have their place, within the order of verses 27-28
decisions.reason: Paul has ranked prophecy higher, but he does not let the church shut out tongues; interpreted and in turn, they too build up the church (verse 5).

decisions.choice: set your hearts on (B); try hard to (R)
decisions.reason: As in 12:31 and 14:1.

records.source: πάντα δὲ εὐσχημόνως καὶ κατὰ τάξιν γινέσθω.
records.gloss: All things but fittingly and according to order let be done.
pieces: But let everything be done properly and in good order.

L.40: But let all things be done fittingly and according to order.

R.40: But make sure that everything is done properly, in an orderly way.

decisions.choice: fittingly: in a way that is proper and becoming
decisions.reason: εὐσχημόνως describes what is seemly and fitting. Its root is the word for the 'presentable' parts of the body in 12:23-24, and it is used in Romans 13:13 and 1 Thessalonians 4:12 of conduct that is fitting before others.

decisions.choice: according to order: in proper sequence, each in turn
decisions.reason: τάξιν is an ordered arrangement, used of priests serving in turn (Luke 1:8). It sums up verses 27-33: one at a time, in turn, as befits the God of peace, not of disorder.

decisions.choice: properly
decisions.reason: 'Decently' now suggests only modesty; the Greek word means what is fitting.
